theory.intro: You can prove a property of a triangle or special quadrilateral from its definition using congruent triangles. Prove two triangles congruent, then use their matching sides or angles to give the property.
facts: Matching (corresponding) sides and angles of **congruent** triangles are equal; this is the step that carries you from congruence to the property.
Useful reasons: **alternate**, **co-interior** and **corresponding** angles on parallel lines; **vertically opposite** angles; **angles on a straight line** add to $180^{\circ}$.
A **definition** gives the least information needed to identify a shape, such as two pairs of parallel sides for a parallelogram.
A rhombus is defined by four equal sides, and a square by four equal sides and a right angle.
To prove two angles meeting on a straight line are each $90^{\circ}$, show they are equal, then use that they add to $180^{\circ}$.
steps: Identify the two triangles that contain the sides or angles named in the property.
Prove the two triangles are congruent, giving a reason for each equal pair of sides or angles and stating the test (SSS, SAS, AAS or RHS).
Use the matching sides or angles of the congruent triangles, with any further angle reasoning, to establish the required property.

workedExamples.solution_text:
In $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle RSP$:
$\angle QPR=\angle SRP$ (alternate angles, $PQ\parallel SR$).
$\angle QRP=\angle SPR$ (alternate angles, $QR\parallel PS$).
$PR$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle PQR\cong\triangle RSP$ (AAS).
Matching sides give $PQ=RS$ and $QR=SP$.
Matching angles give $\angle PQR=\angle RSP$.
For the other pair, add the equal angles at the ends of the diagonal:
$\begin{aligned}\angle SPQ&=\angle SPR+\angle RPQ\\&=\angle QRP+\angle PRS\\&=\angle QRS.\end{aligned}$
Both pairs of opposite sides and opposite angles are equal.

In $\triangle JKN$ and $\triangle LMN$:
$\angle KJN=\angle MLN$ (alternate angles, $JK\parallel ML$).
$\angle JKN=\angle LMN$ (alternate angles, $JK\parallel ML$).
$JK=LM$ (opposite sides of a parallelogram).
Therefore $\triangle JKN\cong\triangle LMN$ (AAS).
$JN=LN$ and $KN=MN$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).
Each diagonal is divided into two equal parts, so the diagonals bisect each other.

In $\triangle XYT$ and $\triangle XZT$:
$XY=XZ$ (given).
$YT=ZT$ ($T$ is the midpoint).
$XT$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle XYT\cong\triangle XZT$ (SSS).
$\angle XTY=\angle XTZ$ (matching angles of congruent triangles).
$\angle XTY+\angle XTZ=180^{\circ}$ (angles on the straight line $YZ$).
The equal angles each measure $90^{\circ}$, so $XT\perp YZ$.

a. In $\triangle JKL$ and $\triangle JML$:
$JK=JM$ and $LK=LM$ (given).
$JL$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle JKL\cong\triangle JML$ (SSS).
$\angle JKL=\angle JML$ (matching angles of congruent triangles).

b. The same congruence gives $\angle KJL=\angle MJL$ and $\angle KLJ=\angle MLJ$.
Thus $JL$ bisects both vertex angles.

c. In $\triangle JKN$ and $\triangle JMN$:
$JK=JM$ (given).
$\angle KJN=\angle MJN$ (proved in part b).
$JN$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle JKN\cong\triangle JMN$ (SAS).
$\angle JNK=\angle JNM$ (matching angles).
These angles add to $180^{\circ}$ on the straight line $KM$, so each is $90^{\circ}$. Hence $JL\perp KM$.

a. In $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle PSR$:
$PQ=PS$ and $RQ=RS$ (equal sides of a rhombus).
$PR$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle PQR\cong\triangle PSR$ (SSS).
$\angle QPR=\angle SPR$ and $\angle QRP=\angle SRP$ (matching angles).
Thus $PR$ bisects both vertex angles.

b. In $\triangle PQN$ and $\triangle PSN$:
$PQ=PS$ (equal sides of a rhombus).
$QN=SN$ (diagonals bisect each other).
$PN$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle PQN\cong\triangle PSN$ (SSS).
$\angle PNQ=\angle PNS$ (matching angles).
These angles add to $180^{\circ}$ on the straight line $QS$, so each is $90^{\circ}$. Hence $PR\perp QS$.

a. In $\triangle JKL$ and $\triangle MLK$:
$JK=ML$ (equal sides of a square).
$\angle JKL=\angle MLK=90^{\circ}$ (right angles of a square).
$KL$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle JKL\cong\triangle MLK$ (SAS).
$JL=MK$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).

b. A square is a parallelogram, so $JN=LN$ and $KN=MN$.
In $\triangle JKN$ and $\triangle LKN$:
$JK=LK$ (equal sides of a square).
$JN=LN$ (diagonals bisect each other).
$KN$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle JKN\cong\triangle LKN$ (SSS).
$\angle JNK=\angle LNK$ (matching angles).
These angles add to $180^{\circ}$ on the straight line $JL$, so each is $90^{\circ}$.
The diagonals bisect each other at right angles.

In $\triangle XYT$ and $\triangle XZT$:
$\angle XTY=\angle XTZ=90^{\circ}$ ($XT\perp YZ$).
$\angle YXT=\angle ZXT$ (given).
$XT$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle XYT\cong\triangle XZT$ (AAS).
$XY=XZ$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).
The triangle has two equal sides, so it is isosceles.

In $\triangle XYT$ and $\triangle XZT$:
$XY=XZ$ (given).
$\angle YXT=\angle ZXT$ ($XT$ bisects the apex angle).
$XT$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle XYT\cong\triangle XZT$ (SAS).
$YT=ZT$ (matching sides), so $XT$ bisects the base.
$\angle XTY=\angle XTZ$ (matching angles).
These angles add to $180^{\circ}$ on the straight line $YZ$, so each is $90^{\circ}$. Hence $XT\perp YZ$.

$\angle MJK+\angle JML=180^{\circ}$ because both are right angles. Hence $JK\parallel ML$ (converse of the co-interior angle property).
Similarly, $\angle MJK+\angle JKL=180^{\circ}$, so $JM\parallel KL$.
In $\triangle JKL$ and $\triangle LMJ$:
$\angle KJL=\angle MLJ$ (alternate angles, $JK\parallel ML$).
$\angle KLJ=\angle MJL$ (alternate angles, $KL\parallel JM$).
$JL$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle JKL\cong\triangle LMJ$ (AAS).
$JK=LM$ and $KL=MJ$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).

In $\triangle JKL$ and $\triangle LMJ$:
$JK=LM$ and $KL=MJ$ (given).
$JL$ is common.
Therefore $\triangle JKL\cong\triangle LMJ$ (SSS).
$\angle KJL=\angle MLJ$ (matching angles), so $JK\parallel LM$ (converse of the alternate angle property).
$\angle KLJ=\angle MJL$ (matching angles), so $KL\parallel MJ$ (converse of the alternate angle property).
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $JKLM$ is a parallelogram.

In $\triangle JKN$ and $\triangle LMN$:
$JN=LN$ and $KN=MN$ (given).
$\angle JNK=\angle LNM$ (vertically opposite angles).
Therefore $\triangle JKN\cong\triangle LMN$ (SAS).
$\angle JKN=\angle LMN$ (matching angles), so $JK\parallel LM$ (converse of the alternate angle property).

In $\triangle JMN$ and $\triangle LKN$:
$JN=LN$ and $MN=KN$ (given).
$\angle JNM=\angle LNK$ (vertically opposite angles).
Therefore $\triangle JMN\cong\triangle LKN$ (SAS).
$\angle JMN=\angle LKN$ (matching angles), so $JM\parallel LK$ (converse of the alternate angle property).
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $JKLM$ is a parallelogram.

foundation.solution_text:
In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$:
$\angle BAC = \angle DCA$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$)
$\angle BCA = \angle DAC$ (alternate angles, $AD \parallel BC$)
$AC$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ (AAS)
$\therefore AB = DC$ and $BC = DA$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)
So the opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.

In $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CDB$:
$\angle ABD = \angle CDB$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$)
$\angle ADB = \angle CBD$ (alternate angles, $AD \parallel BC$)
$BD$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABD \cong \triangle CDB$ (AAS)
$\therefore \angle DAB = \angle BCD$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
$\angle ABC = \angle ABD + \angle DBC = \angle CDB + \angle BDA = \angle ADC$
So the opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.

In $\triangle ABE$ and $\triangle CDE$:
$\angle BAE = \angle DCE$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$)
$\angle ABE = \angle CDE$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$)
$AB = DC$ (opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal)
$\therefore \triangle ABE \cong \triangle CDE$ (AAS)
$\therefore AE = CE$ and $BE = DE$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)
So the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

In $\triangle PQN$ and $\triangle PRN$:
$PQ = PR$ (given)
$QN = RN$ ($N$ is the midpoint of $QR$)
$PN$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle PQN \cong \triangle PRN$ (SSS)
$\therefore \angle PNQ = \angle PNR$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
$\angle PNQ + \angle PNR = 180^{\circ}$ (angles on a straight line)
$\therefore \angle PNQ = \angle PNR = 90^{\circ}$
So $PN$ is perpendicular to $QR$.

In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ADC$:
$AB = AD$ (sides of a rhombus are equal)
$CB = CD$ (sides of a rhombus are equal)
$AC$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADC$ (SSS)
$\therefore \angle BAC = \angle DAC$ and $\angle BCA = \angle DCA$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
So the diagonal $AC$ bisects $\angle A$ and $\angle C$.

In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle DCB$:
$AB = DC$ (sides of a square are equal)
$\angle ABC = \angle DCB = 90^{\circ}$ (angles of a square are right angles)
$BC$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABC \cong \triangle DCB$ (SAS)
$\therefore AC = DB$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)
So the diagonals of a square are equal.

In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ADC$:
$AB = AD$ (equal sides of a kite)
$CB = CD$ (equal sides of a kite)
$AC$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADC$ (SSS)
$\therefore \angle ABC = \angle ADC$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
So one pair of opposite angles of a kite is equal.

In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ADC$:
$AB = AD$ (equal sides of a kite)
$CB = CD$ (equal sides of a kite)
$AC$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABC \cong \triangle ADC$ (SSS)
$\therefore \angle BAC = \angle DAC$ and $\angle BCA = \angle DCA$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
So the diagonal $AC$ bisects $\angle BAD$ and $\angle BCD$.

In $\triangle PQN$ and $\triangle PRN$:
$\angle PNQ = \angle PNR = 90^{\circ}$ ($PN \perp QR$)
$\angle QPN = \angle NPR$ (given)
$PN$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle PQN \cong \triangle PRN$ (AAS)
$\therefore PQ = PR$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)
So $\triangle PQR$ is isosceles because it has two equal sides.

In $\triangle PQN$ and $\triangle PRN$:
$PQ = PR$ (given)
$\angle QPN = \angle NPR$ ($PN$ bisects $\angle QPR$)
$PN$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle PQN \cong \triangle PRN$ (SAS)
$\therefore \angle PNQ = \angle PNR$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
$\angle PNQ + \angle PNR = 180^{\circ}$ (angles on a straight line $QR$)
$\therefore \angle PNQ = \angle PNR = 90^{\circ}$
So $PN$ is perpendicular to $QR$.

$\angle DAB = \angle ADC = 90^{\circ}$ (angles of a rectangle), and $\angle DAB + \angle ADC = 180^{\circ}$, so $AB \parallel DC$ (co-interior angles supplementary).
Similarly $AD \parallel BC$.
In $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$:
$\angle BAC = \angle DCA$ (alternate angles, $AB \parallel DC$)
$\angle BCA = \angle DAC$ (alternate angles, $AD \parallel BC$)
$AC$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA$ (AAS)
$\therefore AB = DC$ and $BC = DA$ (matching sides of congruent triangles)
So the opposite sides of a rectangle are equal.

mastery.solution_text:
In $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle RSP$:
$PQ = RS$ (given)
$QR = SP$ (given)
$PR$ is common.
$\therefore \triangle PQR \cong \triangle RSP$ (SSS)
$\therefore \angle QPR = \angle SRP$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
$\therefore PQ \parallel RS$ (equal alternate angles)
Also $\angle QRP = \angle SPR$ (matching angles of congruent triangles)
$\therefore QR \parallel PS$ (equal alternate angles)
So $PQRS$ is a parallelogram because both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.
